## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ This study explores the relationships between teachers' artificial intelligence literacy (AIL), AI-TPACK compe-

Artificial intelligence literacy tencies, job satisfaction, and well-being. Survey data from 350 in-service teachers were analyzed using PLS-SEM AI-TPACK to examine how AI-related competencies are associated with professional and psychological outcomes. The teacher satisfaction

findings reveal that AIL strongly predicts AI-specific knowledge, especially AI-TCK, AI-TK, AI-TPCK, and AI-TPK, 

teacher well-being structural equation modeling with a moderate influence on traditional pedagogical knowledge. At the job satisfaction level, AI-TCK and 

general pedagogical knowledge are positively associated with satisfaction, while AI-TK has a negative rela- tionship. Mediation analyses show that AI competencies influence well-being through job satisfaction. AI-TCK and pedagogical knowledge are positively associated with well-being indirectly through job satisfaction, whereas AI-TK shows a negative indirect association along the same pathway. The study suggests that AI-related competencies are linked to teachers' work-life outcomes, and highlights job satisfaction as the key mediator between AI competence and well-being. Because the design is cross-sectional and self-reported, these relation- ships are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The study advocates for integrating AI in ways 

that support pedagogical development rather than just technical skills.

The Turkish context adds additional relevance to the study. AI lit- eracy competencies have recently been added to the K-12 curriculum in Turkey, creating new expectations for practicing teachers. However, the evidence suggests that teachers, particularly those in non-STEM fields and those working in disadvantaged regions, continue to show notable gaps in both AIL and AI-TPACK ([Banaz & Demirel, 2024;](#51-limitations-and-future-research) Karayigit et al., ˘ 2025). At the same time, AI-assisted tools are becoming more common in classrooms, but they are not matched by adequate, structured pro- fessional development. Turkey, therefore, offers a particularly useful context for examining how AI competencies relate to professional and psychological outcomes.

## 2. Theoretical framework

The relationships examined in this study span three qualitatively distinct transitions: from AI literacy to AI-related competence, from competence to job satisfaction, and from job satisfaction to well-being. No single theory explains all three equally well. Following recent teacher research that integrates multiple frameworks by specifying the distinct contribution of each rather than invoking them interchangeably (Chen, Dang, & Zhang, 2026; Chen, He, et al., 2026; Ning, 2026), the present model treats Social Cognitive Theory, the Job Demands–Resources model, and Self-Determination Theory as comple- mentary rather than competing accounts. Each governs one link in a single sequential chain, and none alone accounts for the full pathway from AI literacy to teacher well-being.

Social Cognitive Theory (SCT; [Bandura, 1986)](#51-limitations-and-future-research) explains the first transition: how AIL develops into AI-TPACK competencies. The Job Demands–Resources model (JD-R; [Bakker & Demerouti, 2017)](#51-limitations-and-future-research) explains the second: why specific competence components, once acquired, function differentially as resources or demands for job satisfaction. Self- Determination Theory (SDT; Ryan & Deci, 2000, 2017) explains the third: how the resulting job satisfaction translates into the emotional, psychological, and social dimensions of well-being. AI-TPACK is not a fourth theory but the structural scaffold that defines the competence constructs connecting the first transition to the second. Because each theory is confined to a single link, the comparatively large number of hypothesized paths does not reflect an accumulation of theories. It follows from one sequential logic: a fixed set of competence constructs is first predicted from AIL (seven paths, H1–H7), then eval- uated as job resources or job demands with respect to job satisfaction (seven paths, H8–H14), and finally transmitted through job satisfaction to three well-being outcomes (three paths, H15–H17). [Table 1](#2-theoretical-framework) makes this mapping explicit.

Social Cognitive Theory (SCT; [Bandura, 1986)](#51-limitations-and-future-research) addresses the first developmental mechanism linking AIL to AI-TPACK. The Job Demands–Resources model (JD-R; [Bakker & Demerouti, 2017)](#51-limitations-and-future-research) ad- dresses the second professional dynamics linking AI-TPACK to job satisfaction. Self-Determination Theory (SDT; Ryan & Deci, 2000, 2017) addresses the third the psychological mechanism linking job satisfaction to well-being. AI-TPACK is not treated here as a fourth independent theory but as the structural scaffold within which these three theoretical explanations are situated. Together, they provide a coherent and

### _2.1._ _From TPACK to AI-TPACK: qualitative reconceptualization_

Before establishing AI-TPACK's role in the model, it is worth explaining why standard TPACK falls short in this context. The TPACK model holds that effective teaching requires integrating content knowledge (CK), pedagogical knowledge (PK), and technological knowledge (TK) (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The problem is that TPACK's TK component was designed with general educational technologies in mind, and only partially captures what AI integration demands of teachers (Weidlich & Kalz, 2023).

AI differs from conventional educational technologies in several important ways. Its decision processes are often opaque. Its output re- quires careful teacher evaluation. Every use carries both pedagogical and ethical responsibility. Moreover, human–AI interaction demands continuous adaptation and judgment rather than routine tool operation (Cheng et al., 2025; Wagner et al., 2024).

These differences mean that TPACK's TK component cannot fully capture AI-specific competencies. AI-TPACK addresses this gap by treating AI-related knowledge as a set of distinct components: AI tech- nological knowledge (AI-TK), AI technological content knowledge (AI- TCK), AI technological pedagogical knowledge (AI-TPK), and AI tech- nological pedagogical content knowledge (AI-TPCK), the latter repre- senting the highest-order synthesis of these components (Ning et al., 2024). To avoid ambiguity, we use AI-TPACK throughout to denote the overall framework and measurement instrument encompassing all seven knowledge domains, and AI-TPCK to denote the specific higher- order sub-dimension (AI technological pedagogical content knowl- edge) that integrates AI-related technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge. The two terms are therefore not interchangeable: AI-TPACK names the model; AI-TPCK names one construct within it. This is not simply relabeling. Each component reflects a different knowledge domain that AI integration requires of teachers. The findings of this study bear that out; these components show distinct, and in some cases opposing, effects on job satisfaction. AI-TPACK should therefore be treated as an independent conceptual framework rather than a renamed extension of TPACK ([Celik, 2023)](#51-limitations-and-future-research).

### _2.2._ _From AIL to AI-TPACK: social cognitive theory_

How AIL develops AI-TPACK competencies is explained through Social Cognitive Theory (SCT; [Bandura, 1986)](#51-limitations-and-future-research). SCT holds that compe- tence develops through the interaction of cognitive, behavioral, and environmental factors, with self-efficacy beliefs playing a central mediating role.

In the context of AI integration, this mechanism operates through three theoretical channels. First, teachers who can critically evaluate AI tools and adapt them for pedagogical purposes develop stronger self- efficacy beliefs in their capacity to use them effectively. This creates a foundation for goal-directed professional practice through which AI- TPACK components, AI-TK, AI-TCK, and AI-TPK, are gradually 

consolidated. Second, SCT's emphasis on observational learning suggests that teachers with higher AIL interpret peer practices more perceptively and develop richer cognitive schemas for pedagogical decision-making (Rütti-Joy et al., 2023). This process activates not only AI-TPACK components but also traditional knowledge domains such as PK, PCK, and SK, which is why the hypotheses about AIL's effects on these con- structs have theoretical grounding. Third, SCT's self-regulation dimen- sion positions AIL as a cognitive resource that enables teachers to continuously monitor and reorganize their AI-TPACK competencies in relation to pedagogical goals.

Taken together, AIL is not simply a knowledge base. It functions as a self-regulatory resource that activates broader pedagogical knowledge structures within AI-integrated teaching environments. Based on this reasoning, the following hypotheses are proposed: 

**H1**. Teachers' AIL has a positive and significant effect on AI-TCK.

**H2**. Teachers' AIL has a positive and significant effect on AI-TK.

**H3**. Teachers' AIL has a positive and significant effect on AI-TPCK.

**H4**. Teachers' AIL has a positive and significant effect on AI-TPK.

**H5**. Teachers' AIL has a positive and significant effect on PCK.

**H6**. Teachers' AIL has a positive and significant effect on PK.

**H7**. Teachers' AIL has a positive and significant effect on SK.

### _2.3._ _From AI-TPACK to job satisfaction: the job demands_–_resources model_

The relationship between AI-TPACK components and job satisfaction is not uniform. It is component-specific and differentiated, and the theoretical logic for this differentiation is grounded in the Job Demands–Resources model (JD-R; [Bakker & Demerouti, 2017)](#51-limitations-and-future-research). The JD- R model distinguishes between job resources, which support motivation, job satisfaction, and goal attainment, and job demands, which require sustained effort and are associated with strain. Pedagogical competence, professional self-efficacy, and autonomy are among the core resources that support job satisfaction (Lauermann & Konig, ¨ 2016; Skaalvik & Skaalvik, 2014).

Within this framework, AI-TPACK components do not all occupy the same position on the resource-demand continuum. AI-TCK, knowledge of how AI tools relate to specific subject content, helps teachers select pedagogically meaningful AI applications in their own domains. It re- duces uncertainty and strengthens the sense of professional competence, functioning as a cognitive resource. AI-TPK, knowledge of how AI can support pedagogical strategies enables teachers to diversify AI-assisted instructional practices, supporting pedagogical autonomy and a sense of agency. AI-TPCK, as the highest-order integration of these compo- nents, can be read as an indicator of professional mastery and carries the strongest resource value in JD-R terms.

AI-TK, by contrast, purely technical AI knowledge without peda- gogical grounding may function more like a job demand. It can generate adaptation pressure and role ambiguity, which undermines job satis- faction (Tarafdar et al., 2010; Zhang & Cao, 2025). Research on tech- nostress supports this: technically focused knowledge, when unsupported by contextual resources, can weaken job-related ap- praisals. This provides the theoretical basis for expecting a negative relationship between AI-TK and job satisfaction (Huang & Zhao, 2025). Traditional knowledge components, PK, PCK, and SK, carry profes- sional resource value independent of AI. They are therefore conceptu- alized as positively influencing job satisfaction (Nurgaliyeva et al., 2023). Based on this reasoning: 

**H8**. AI-TCK has a significant effect on teachers' job satisfaction.

**H9**. AI-TK has a significant effect on teachers' job satisfaction.

**H10**. AI-TPCK has a significant effect on teachers' job satisfaction.

**H11**. AI-TPK has a significant effect on teachers' job satisfaction.

**H12**. PK has a significant effect on teachers' job satisfaction.

**H13**. PCK has a significant effect on teachers' job satisfaction.

**H14**. SK has a significant effect on teachers' job satisfaction.

### _2.4._ _From job satisfaction to well-being: self-determination theory_

The mechanism through which job satisfaction translates into teacher well-being is explained by Self-Determination Theory (SDT; Ryan & Deci, 2000, 2017). SDT holds that the satisfaction of three basic psychological needs, competence, autonomy, and relatedness, is a uni- versal prerequisite for well-being. In professional contexts, job satis- faction can be understood as a proximal indicator of how well these needs are being met. Recent teacher research likewise grounds moti- vation and well-being in the satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs (Ning, 2026), and the empirical link between auton- omous teaching motivation, job satisfaction, and well-being is well established (Skaalvik & Skaalvik, 2023; Slemp et al., 2018; Van den Broeck et al., 2016).

In this study, job satisfaction is not treated merely as an intermediate outcome. It is the key mechanism that explains how AI-TPACK compe- tencies translate into well-being. When teachers find their professional roles satisfying, all three core psychological needs tend to be met: competence (believing their skills are being used effectively), autonomy (exercising meaningful agency over pedagogical decisions), and relat- edness (building genuine connections with students and colleagues). According to SDT, meeting these needs directly determines emotional, psychological, and social well-being. Job satisfaction, therefore, func- tions as the bridge through which AI-TPACK competencies reach psy- chological outcomes (Dreer, 2023; Maricuțoiu et al., 2023). Teacher well-being itself is treated as a multidimensional construct encompass- ing emotional, psychological, and social dimensions ([Bagdˇziunien¯](#51-limitations-and-future-research) [e ˙](#51-limitations-and-future-research) [et al., 2023;](#51-limitations-and-future-research) Mesurado et al., 2021).

In AI-integrated teaching environments, this mechanism has two faces. On the one hand, role overload, technological complexity, and uncertainty-driven technostress can erode job satisfaction and increase burnout risk (Fern´andez-Batanero et al., 2021; Tarafdar et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2025). On the other hand, AI used in meaningful ways can become a source of motivation, improving both job satisfaction and well-being ([Almaki et al., 2025;](#51-limitations-and-future-research) Skaalvik & Skaalvik, 2020). Job satis- faction thus functions as the central transmission mechanism carrying the effects of AI-TPACK competencies to well-being, positively through some components (AI-TCK, PK) and negatively through others (AI-TK). Based on this reasoning: 

**H15**. Job satisfaction has a positive and significant effect on emotional well-being.

**H16**. Job satisfaction has a positive and significant effect on psycho- logical well-being.

**H17**. Job satisfaction has a positive and significant effect on social well-being.

Taken together, the three theories converge on a single argument: the value of AI competence for teacher well-being is neither automatic nor uniform. Whether a given competence enhances or erodes well- being depends on whether it functions as a job resource or a job de- mand, and this effect reaches well-being only indirectly, through job satisfaction. The model is therefore deliberately constrained: each the- ory is confined to the one transition it explains best, no transition is governed by more than one theory, and well-being is modeled as a distal outcome rather than a direct effect of competence. This parsimony is

what allows a model with many paths to rest on a single, testable explanatory logic.

The relationships underlying these hypotheses are summarized in [Fig. 1,](#3-method) which presents the study's conceptual model.

As presented in [Fig. 1,](#3-method) the hypothesized model follows a sequential path from AIL to AI-related competence domains, from these domains to job satisfaction, and from job satisfaction to well-being. In this model, job satisfaction is specified as a mediating variable linking competence domains to the psychological, social, and emotional dimensions of well- being. In contrast, well-being is conceptualized as the outcome variable.

## 3. Method

### _3.1._ _Research design_

This study examined how teachers' AI literacy (AIL) and AI-TPACK competencies relate to job satisfaction and well-being. A relational survey design was used, which is standard in quantitative research for assessing the direction and degree of covariation among variables (Karasar, 2007). Because the theoretical model included mediation and multiple structural relationships, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to test direct and indirect effects simultaneously ([Byrne, 2013;](#51-limitations-and-future-research) Kline, 2023).

Partial least squares SEM (PLS-SEM) was preferred over covariance- based SEM (CB-SEM) for several reasons: the study's exploratory- predictive orientation, the model's complexity (12 constructs, 17 hy- pothesized paths), incomplete multivariate normality in some variables, and insufficient cross-population invariance evidence for some of the instruments. Given these conditions, PLS-SEM was the more appropriate choice.

### _3.2._ _Participants_

350 teachers working across various provinces in Turkey partici- pated in the study. The sample exceeds the commonly recommended minimum thresholds for SEM (_n_ ≥ 100–150; Kline, 2023) and satisfies the ten-times rule for PLS-SEM. Based on the highest number of struc- tural paths pointing to any single construct, the minimum required sample size was 70 (10 × 7 = 70); the sample of 350 comfortably clears this threshold (Hair et al., 2017).

Convenience sampling was used. Participants were recruited through school administrator networks and professional communication chan- nels via an online survey link. The sample included teachers from 

Conceptual model of the study.

primary, middle, and high school levels, drawn from both STEM and non-STEM subject areas, with varying levels of professional experience. That said, the sample has limitations worth noting. The online dis- tribution likely overrepresented teachers who are already interested in digital technologies and AI, while underrepresenting those in low- connectivity or digitally disadvantaged schools. The absence of detailed subgroup breakdowns by school type, subject area, and years of experience also limits the extent to which the sample's composition can be assessed. Findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously, particularly for teachers with limited AI experience and those working in less resourced settings.

### _3.3._ _Instruments_

Four scales were used: the AI Literacy Scale, the AI-TPACK Scale, the Job Satisfaction Scale, and the Well-Being Scale. Each was selected based on its psychometric properties and fit with the study's theoretical framework.

#### _3.3.1._ _AI literacy scale_

Developed by Wang et al. (2023) and adapted into Turkish by Gokçearslan et al. (2024)¨ , this is a 10-item, four-factor, 5-point Likert scale with an overall Cronbach's alpha of 0.74. It covers AI awareness, AI use and application, AI evaluation, and AI ethics. These dimensions provide empirical grounding for the AIL construct as operationalized here encompassing basic awareness, functional use, and evaluative reasoning. The scale does not fully capture higher-order dimensions such as critical algorithmic literacy, data governance, or institutional ethical accountability, which means AIL in this study is operationalized primarily in functional and evaluative terms.

#### _3.3.2._ _AI-TPACK scale_

Developed by Ning et al. (2024) and adapted into Turkish by [Canbazoglu Bilici et al. (2024)˘](#51-limitations-and-future-research) [,](#51-limitations-and-future-research) this is a 39-item, seven-factor, 5-point Likert scale with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.98. It covers AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, and AI-TPCK, alongside the traditional TPACK components of PK, PCK, and SK. This multi-dimensional structure provides the analytical basis for testing the component-specific differentiated effects proposed in the model.

#### _3.3.3._ _Job satisfaction scale_

Originally developed by [Brayfield and Rothe (1951),](#51-limitations-and-future-research) shortened by Judge et al. (1998), and adapted into Turkish by Keser and Ongen Bilir ¨

(2019), this is a single-factor, 5-item scale with factor loadings ranging from 0.84 to 0.93 and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.92. Its unidimensional structure fits well with the study's treatment of job satisfaction as a mediating variable bridging AI-TPACK competencies and teacher well- being.

#### _3.3.4._ _Well-being scale_

Developed by Mesurado et al. (2021) and adapted into Turkish by Dadandı and Aydın (2025), this is a 12-item, three-factor scale covering social, psychological, and emotional well-being, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.86. The multidimensional structure allows each well-being dimen- sion to be examined separately in relation to the competence, autonomy, and relatedness needs addressed in self-determination theory. It fits directly with the study's theoretical framework.

### _3.4._ _Data collection_

Data were collected online using instruments with previously established validity and reliability. The survey did not request any personally identifying information no names, ID numbers, or institu- tional affiliations. Before completing the survey, participants received an information form explaining the study's purpose and scope, con- firming that data would be used solely for scientific purposes, and providing informed consent. The survey was administered anony- mously, and data was encrypted and stored securely.

### _3.5._ _Analytical procedure_

Analyses followed the two-stage PLS-SEM procedure recommended by Hair et al. (2019). In the first stage, the measurement model was evaluated for reliability (Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability), convergent validity (AVE and factor loadings), and discriminant validity (Fornell–Larcker criterion, cross-loadings, and HTMT). The structural model was examined only after acceptable psychometric properties were confirmed. In the second stage, the structural model was assessed using path coefficients, R2, f2, and Q2 values. The PLS algorithm was estimated in SmartPLS 4.0 using a path weighting scheme with a maximum of 300 iterations. The significance of direct and indirect ef- fects was evaluated through bootstrapping with 5000 subsamples and bias-corrected confidence intervals (Ringle et al., 2014).

### _3.6._ _Assessment of the measurement model: reliability and convergent validity_

Before evaluating the structural model, the measurement model was assessed for internal consistency reliability and convergent validity. Internal consistency reliability was examined using Cronbach's alpha, rho\_A, and composite reliability (CR), whereas convergent validity was evaluated based on indicator loadings and average variance extracted (AVE). In line with established guidelines, factor loadings of 0.70 or higher, Cronbach's alpha and CR values of 0.70 or above, and AVE values of 0.50 or above were considered indicative of acceptable mea- surement quality (Fornell & Larcker, 1981; Hair et al., 2017). Because the data were collected from a single source at a single point in time, the possibility of common method bias was also examined. Following Kock's (2015) full-collinearity approach, variance inflation factor (VIF) values were calculated for all latent constructs. The VIF values ranged from 1.00 to 2.65, remaining well below the conservative threshold of 3.3. These findings suggest that common method bias is unlikely to pose a serious threat to the validity of the results. The original AI-TPACK scale developed by Ning et al. (2024) con- sisted of 39 items across seven sub-dimensions. In the present study, two items from the AIL scale (AIL2, λ = 0.61; AIL8, λ = 0.63) were retained despite loadings below the conventional 0.70 threshold because the construct still met the recommended AVE (0.60) and CR (0.93) criteria, and deleting these items did not improve the measurement properties. 

As noted by Hair et al. (2017), indicators with loadings between 0.40 and 0.70 may be retained when construct-level reliability and conver- gent validity remain satisfactory. In contrast, five items from the AI- TPACK measure (AI-TPK1, AI-TPK5, AI-TCK6, AI-TPCK1, and AI- TPCK2) were removed because they exhibited substantial cross- loadings on theoretically adjacent constructs. This decision was made to improve construct distinctiveness while preserving adequate con- ceptual coverage of the retained dimensions. The results of the reli- ability and convergent validity analyses are presented in [Table 2.](#as-shown-in-table-5-the-models-explanatory-power-varied-consid--erably-across-endogenous-constructs-explained-variance-was-moderate-for-ai-tpck-r2--053-and-ai-tpk-r2--051-and-somewhat-lower) As shown in [Table 2,](#as-shown-in-table-5-the-models-explanatory-power-varied-consid--erably-across-endogenous-constructs-explained-variance-was-moderate-for-ai-tpck-r2--053-and-ai-tpk-r2--051-and-somewhat-lower) Cronbach's alpha values ranged from 0.80 to 0.95, rho\_A values from 0.80 to 0.95, and composite reliability values from 0.87 to 0.96, all of which exceeded the recommended threshold of 0.70. In addition, AVE values ranged from 0.56 to 0.89, indicating that each construct explained more than half of the variance of its indicators. Taken together, these findings support the internal consistency, reli- ability, and convergent validity of the measurement model (Fornell & Larcker, 1981; Hair et al., 2017).

### _3.7._ _Discriminant validity_

Discriminant validity was assessed in three steps: examination of cross-loadings, application of the Fornell–Larcker criterion, and calcu- lation of the heterotrait–monotrait ratio of correlations (HTMT). First, cross-loadings were inspected to determine whether each indicator loaded more strongly on its intended construct than on any other construct. Because high cross-loadings may indicate conceptual overlap and weaken construct distinctiveness, items AI-TPK1, AI-TPK5, AI- TCK6, AI-TPCK1, and AI-TPCK2 were excluded from further analysis (Hair et al., 2019; Kline, 2023). This item-removal procedure was applied to strengthen the psychometric clarity of the measurement model and to reduce inter-construct contamination.

Second, discriminant validity was evaluated using the For- nell–Larcker criterion. According to this criterion, the square root of a construct's AVE should exceed its correlations with all other constructs in the model (Fornell & Larcker, 1981). Results are presented in Table 3. As reported in Table 3, this condition was satisfied for all constructs, indicating that each construct shared more variance with its own in- dicators than with other latent variables in the model. These results provide evidence of adequate discriminant validity, consistent with the Fornell–Larcker criterion (Fornell & Larcker, 1981).

Third, HTMT values were calculated as a more stringent assessment of discriminant validity in PLS-SEM. HTMT values below 0.90 are generally considered acceptable for theoretically related constructs (Hair et al., 2017; Henseler et al., 2015). Results are presented in Table 4.

As shown in Table 4, all HTMT values remained below this threshold, with the highest value observed for the AI-TK/AI-TCK pair (HTMT = 0.870). Discriminant validity was therefore established for all construct pairs (Hair et al., 2017; Henseler et al., 2015). The relatively higher HTMT values among AI-TPACK-related dimensions are theoretically expected, given the intersecting and conceptually related nature of the TPACK framework and are consistent with prior empirical work (Ning et al., 2024; Schmidt et al., 2009). Evidence from cross-loadings, the Fornell–Larcker criterion, and HTMT together support the discriminant validity of the measurement model.

### _3.8._ _Findings_

This section presents the structural model results. In the proposed model, AIL was specified as the exogenous construct; AI-related and traditional pedagogical knowledge domains served as intermediate predictors; job satisfaction was modeled as the central mediator; and emotional, psychological, and social well-being were treated as outcome variables. Fig. 2 presents the structural model. **Table 2** Reliability and convergent validity.

The structural model was evaluated for collinearity, explanatory power, effect sizes, and predictive relevance. The significance of the structural paths was assessed using bootstrapping with 5000 sub- samples. The VIF, R2, f2, and Q2 values used to evaluate the adequacy of the model and the strength of the hypothesized relationships are pre- sented in Table 5.

### As shown in Table 5, the model's explanatory power varied consid- erably across endogenous constructs. Explained variance was moderate for AI-TPCK (R2 = 0.53) and AI-TPK (R2 = 0.51), and somewhat lower 

but still substantial for AI-TCK (R2 = 0.43) and AI-TK (R2 = 0.43). The R2 values for PCK (R2 = 0.10), PK (R2 = 0.13), SK (R2 = 0.16), and job satisfaction (R2 = 0.11) were limited. For the well-being dimensions, the model accounted for 18% of the variance in emotional well-being, 46% in psychological well-being, and 32% in social well-being. The model performed better in explaining AI-related competence domains than job satisfaction or well-being outcomes.

Among the traditional knowledge components, well-being (β = 0.18, _p_ = .01), psychological well-being (β = 0.28, p _\<_ only PK had a positive, significant effect on job satisfaction. PCK and SK .001), and social well-being (β = 0.23, p _\<_ .001). PK similarly showed did not. AI-TPCK and AI-TPK despite representing more integrated, significant positive indirect effects across all three well-being higher-order competencies also did not significantly predict job satisfaction. These findings suggest that professional satisfaction may depend less on possessing differentiated knowledge structures and more on whether teachers experience a general sense of pedagogical mastery that they can enact in daily practice. Teachers may possess integrative AI-related knowledge yet still be unable to convert it into rewarding professional outcomes because of infrastructure constraints, limited time, or restricted opportunities for classroom implementation. The findings, therefore, qualify for more optimistic assumptions that greater AI-TPACK competence will necessarily yield positive professional out- comes. Read through the job demands–resources lens, these null effects are informative rather than merely absent: a competence confers resource value for job satisfaction only when it is enactable in daily practice, so higher-order or traditional knowledge that teachers cannot readily deploy because of time, infrastructure, or opportunity con- straints neither adds resources nor imposes demands, and its net asso- ciation with satisfaction approaches zero. A parallel pattern appears in recent work using a different but related framework: Chen, Dang, and Zhang (2026), drawing on Conservation of Resources theory with Vietnamese teachers, found that teacher stress had no significant direct link to AI teaching beliefs, whereas teaching enjoyment carried the ef- fect of organizational support. Their finding that an affective- –experiential pathway, not a stress pathway, drove AI-related outcomes converges with ours: what shapes the professional value of AI compe- tence is whether it is experienced as enabling and satisfying, not the mere presence or absence of knowledge or strain.

The final stage of the model showed that job satisfaction had sig- nificant positive effects on emotional, psychological, and social well- being. This indicates that AI-related and pedagogical competencies contribute to teacher well-being primarily through the quality of teachers' professional experience rather than through direct pathways. That said, the predictive relevance values for some well-being outcomes remained weak, and the model explained only a portion of the variance. Teacher well-being is shaped by personal, organizational, and contex- tual factors that this model does not capture. Even so, the consistent effects of job satisfaction across all three well-being dimensions support its role as a central proximal mechanism linking professional compe- tence to broader psychological outcomes.

These limits warrant explicit acknowledgment given the prominence the study assigns to well-being. The explained variance in job satisfac- tion was low (R2 = 0.11), and the out-of-sample predictive relevance for the well-being dimensions was at or near zero (Q2 ≈ 0.00 for emotional, psychological, and social well-being), even though the standardized paths from job satisfaction to well-being were substantial and signifi- cant. This combination indicates that job satisfaction is reliably _associ-_ _ated_ with the well-being outcomes within this sample but is far from a sufficient _predictor_ of them: most of the variance in teacher well-being lies outside the competence-and-satisfaction chain modeled here. We therefore frame well-being not as an outcome the present model ex- plains, but as one it links to job satisfaction, with the larger share of its determinants personal, relational, and organizational remaining outside the model. Claims about well-being should be read accordingly. The mediation findings reinforce this picture. AI-TCK and PK showed positive indirect effects on well-being through job satisfaction; AI-TK showed negative indirect effects. Competence becomes beneficial when it strengthens teachers' sense of effectiveness and professional satisfaction and may become detrimental when it adds pressure without providing corresponding pedagogical or organizational support. This pattern aligns with both self-determination theory and the job demands–resources model, both of which stress the importance of pro- fessionally supportive conditions for sustaining well-being. The study makes three main contributions. First, AIL is most strongly associated with AI-specific competence domains, supporting its role as a foundational antecedent of AI-related pedagogical integration. Second, the effects of competence on job satisfaction are differentiated rather 

than uniform: pedagogically meaningful competence functions as a resource; technically oriented competence may function as a demand. Third, job satisfaction is the principal mechanism through which selected competence domains shape teacher well-being. From a prac- tical standpoint, professional development for AI integration should move beyond technical skill training. Greater emphasis should be placed on developing AI-TCK and broader pedagogical competence, alongside institutional conditions that reduce workload pressure, support imple- mentation, and strengthen professional resources. Without this, increased technological capacity may amplify role strain rather than improve satisfaction and well-being.

## 5. Conclusion and implications

This study examined how teachers' AIL, AI-related competence do- mains, job satisfaction, and well-being connect within an integrated structural model. AIL was a strong predictor of AI-specific pedagogical knowledge domains; its effects on traditional knowledge domains were weaker. The pathway from AI-TPACK to job satisfaction was differen- tiated: AI-TCK showed a positive effect, AI-TK showed a negative effect, and AI-TPCK, AI-TPK, PCK, and SK did not reach significance. These non-significant relationships are not simply null findings. They suggest that possessing integrated or higher-order competencies does not auto- matically translate into professional satisfaction, particularly when contextual conditions limit enactment in daily practice.

Theoretically, the study positions AIL beyond narrow technical proficiency, treating it instead as an antecedent structure that supports pedagogical reasoning, critical evaluation, and ethical responsibility in AI-supported instructional contexts. The findings extend the AI-TPACK literature by showing that the effects of AI-related competence on teacher outcomes are not uniformly positive and are often mediated by professional satisfaction. More specifically, the study integrates AI- TPACK with job demands–resources and self-determination perspec- tives, demonstrating that competence matters not only for instructional integration but also for how teachers experience their roles and well- being.

Three specific contributions follow. First, AI-related competence domains exert differential, and in one case opposing, effects on job satisfaction, challenging the assumption that greater AI knowledge is uniformly beneficial. Second, job satisfaction is the key proximal mechanism linking selected competence domains to emotional, psy- chological, and social well-being. Third, higher-order AI-TPACK di- mensions do not necessarily yield professional benefits unless teachers can enact them within supportive institutional conditions. Together, these findings support a more balanced view of AI integration: one that acknowledges both its pedagogical potential and its professional costs. From an applied perspective, professional development for AI inte- gration should not focus solely on technical exposure or tool use. It should prioritize pedagogically grounded competencies, particularly AI- TCK and broader pedagogical knowledge, while creating organizational conditions that reduce workload pressure, clarify role expectations, and support classroom enactment. Subject-specific lesson design workshops, collaborative communities of practice, and structured reflection on ethical and data-related issues may be especially useful. At the institu- tional and policy levels, the success of AI integration should be measured not only by adoption and proficiency, but also by teachers' professional satisfaction and well-being. Sustainable AI integration requires not only competent teachers but also supportive environments.

Two implications follow specifically from the AI-TK finding and require careful framing. First, because the negative association between AI-TK and job satisfaction is correlational and likely context-dependent, it should not be read as a reason to limit teachers' technical AI knowl- edge. The more defensible reading is that technical training delivered in isolation without subject-specific application or implementation support 

risks adding strain; the practical response is to embed technical content within pedagogical and subject contexts (i.e., to develop AI-TK and AI- TCK together), not to reduce it. Second, AI literacy training itself may help manage the strain that technical knowledge can introduce. Ozbay ¨ (2026) reports that the evaluative dimension of AI literacy is associ- ated with lower technostress, suggesting that programs which build critical, reflective AI literacy rather than tool operation alone can buffer technology-related stress. Teacher professional development might therefore pair subject-specific AI lesson design with explicit attention to critical evaluation, data and ethical reasoning, and coping strategies for technostress, so that growing technical capacity is accompanied by the pedagogical framing and emotional resources that keep it from becoming a demand.

### _5.1._ _Limitations and future research_

Several limitations bear on how these findings should be interpreted. The cross-sectional design and reliance on self-report measures preclude causal or directional inference. Accordingly, all structural paths including the negative AI-TK pathway should be read as associations rather than as effects in which AI competence improves or reduces well- being. The temporal ordering implied by the model is theoretical, not empirically established. The sample's contextual diversity, across school types, regions, and levels of organizational support, limits generaliz- ability. The model also does not include moderating variables that could explain why AI integration benefits some teachers while disadvantaging others. The contrasting effects of AI-TCK and AI-TK on job satisfaction suggest that the professional consequences of AI competence are likely context-dependent.

Several boundary conditions remain underexplored. Leadership support, school climate, workload, role overload, and access to AI infrastructure may all shape whether teachers can convert AI-related competence into positive professional outcomes. Policy pressure and accountability expectations may interact with teachers' sense of auton- omy. Individual differences in technostress may influence whether technically demanding AI knowledge feels motivating or burdensome. Measuring technostress directly, alongside teaching enjoyment and other affective states, would allow future work to test whether the AI- TK–satisfaction association is mediated by strain or by the absence of positive professional emotion, as suggested by Chen, Dang, and Zhang (2026). Future research should examine these contextual and personal conditions more directly.

A further limitation concerns the AIL scale used here. Although it captures foundational awareness, applied use, and evaluative reasoning, it does not fully reflect higher-order dimensions such as critical algo- rithmic literacy, data governance, and institutional ethical account- ability. This may partly explain the modest effects of AIL on traditional pedagogical knowledge domains. In addition, high intercorrelations among some AI-TPACK sub-constructs, together with the removal of cross-loading items, suggest these dimensions may not be fully separable in this sample. This reduces the interpretability of individual path co- efficients and indicates that the findings may partly reflect the broader configuration of AI-TPACK rather than fully distinct sub-dimensions. Because the inner VIF values for these predictors exceeded the con- ventional threshold, the individual path coefficients linking AI-TPACK components to job satisfaction should be interpreted with correspond- ing caution, and the relative magnitudes of these specific effects treated as provisional.

Future studies should use more comprehensive measures of AIL, test higher-order AI-TPACK structures, and employ longitudinal, multilevel, or quasi-experimental designs. Such approaches would allow more direct testing of moderation pathways and help clarify whether the positive and negative effects identified here hold as AI becomes more deeply embedded in teaching practice. Overall, the study contributes to the field by showing that teachers' AI-related competencies should be understood not only in terms of instructional integration but also in 

relation to professional satisfaction, well-being, and the conditions that shape their consequences.
